statement: A cylindrical water tank has an inside diameter of 1 m and a height of 120 cm. It is two-thirds full. How many litres of water does it hold? (1 litre is 1000 cubic centimetres.)

choices.misconception: I found 0.2 pi cubic metres correctly but thought 1 cubic metre is 100 litres.
I worked out the volume of the whole tank and forgot that it is only two-thirds full.
I used the diameter of 1 m as the radius.
I found 0.2 pi cubic metres correctly but thought 1 cubic metre is 10000 litres.

hints: Put every length into the same unit before you multiply.

The volume of a cylinder is pi times the radius squared times the height. Use one unit throughout, take two-thirds, then convert to litres. One cubic decimetre is exactly one litre, which makes decimetres convenient.
In decimetres the radius is 5 and the height is 12.

solutions.reliable: In decimetres the radius is 5 and the height is 12, so the full tank holds pi x 25 x 12 = 300 pi cubic decimetres. Two-thirds of that is 200 pi cubic decimetres, and 1 cubic decimetre is 1 litre, so the tank holds 200 pi litres, about 628 litres. The transferable idea: convert to one unit at the start, and re-read the question for words like diameter and two-thirds before choosing.
solutions.elegant: Working in decimetres makes the final conversion vanish: a cubic decimetre is exactly a litre, so there is nothing left to convert at the end.

whyOnTest: Each distractor is a real slip with units or with re-reading: radius versus diameter, the fill fraction, or how many litres make a cubic metre.
